title: White spectators, dress, and when the dances ended
summary: White people came to watch; she describes the dress, says she was a girl of 13 or 14, and George recalls Grand Army events.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: I just wondered if those dances were something for the tourist people to go to see? Or did any white people go around to watch it?

Yes, indeed. By the drove, white people would go. It was really nice. It was comical, you know. And it really was nice to see them people dancing with the guinea blue dress and the check apron, linen check. Not cotton check. And the chillon. You know, the old head hangar. Oh, yes. It was fixed up nice like a hat. They didn't wear plenty. Old folks didn't wear plenty hats.
How old were you when you saw that?
I was old enough to remember. I don't remember exactly my age, but I was old enough to run off and go see Don Scrayola.
Just a little girl still going to school?
I was old enough to go and see it all right.
Well, as you say, it got so modern, so modern, so modern.
Did it last until, say, the turn of the century? Until 1900? After George was born, did they have them at home?
Oh, no. George wasn't born. I was about 13 or 14 years old.
No, honestly, you used to have that when I was a boy. You used to have what they called it. Grand Army.
Grand Army. Grand Army was on Claiborne.
The memorial. They have something down in Chalmette now. Yeah. They didn't watch.
It was on Claiborne between Oiseline and Bayou Road. It used to be called Bayou Road Street. Then, now they call it Governor Nicholas.
